drapeaux.note: « médecin légiste de l'État » rendu par « the state's forensic pathologist » ; « coroner » ou « medical examiner » possibles selon le statut exact.

titre: Six Minutes of Silence Before Taking a Heart
accroche: On the night of December 2–3, 1967, in Cape Town, a surgical team waits for a donor's heart to stop before daring to remove it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the night of December 2–3, 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town, a surgical team waits, motionless, for a young woman's heart to stop beating. Denise Darvall, 25, has just been hit by a car; she has a brain injury that a neurosurgeon judges hopeless. A few yards away, Louis Washkansky, 53, a diabetic, is waiting too: suffering from severe coronary disease, he is in severe heart failure. The heart that is about to stop will be transplanted into his chest before morning.

## A Technique Already Ready

The surgical procedure is not improvised. Christiaan Barnard and his brother Marius trained on dogs, using a method described in London in 1959 and then developed at Stanford University by Norman Shumway. During a stay in Richmond, Virginia, Barnard also worked in the laboratory of Richard Lower, who had himself been trained by Shumway. Connecting the great vessels and the atria of a new heart to what remains of the old one: surgery, in 1967, already knows how to do it.

## A Death No Law Yet Knows How to Define

The obstacle lies elsewhere. No law, in South Africa or anywhere in the world, yet defines brain death: the definition of brain death proposed by a Harvard Medical School committee will not be published until August 5, 1968, eight months after that night. To take no legal risk, Barnard brings the state's forensic pathologist into the operating room. The team disconnects Denise Darvall's ventilator and waits, about six minutes, for her heart to stop on its own. Only after the pathologist certifies death do the surgeons open the chest and remove the heart.

## The Problem That Remained Whole

The operation lasts nearly five hours. The donor's heart, defibrillated, at first resumes beating only weakly: it takes three attempts to wean it off the heart-lung machine before the blood pressure holds. Afterward, Washkansky's edema subsides quickly and, for nearly two weeks, everything seems to hold. Then infiltrates appear in his lungs. The team interprets them as the onset of rejection and increases the immunosuppressants, which worsens the infection that should have been treated. Washkansky dies on December 21, eighteen days after the operation, of pneumonia and sepsis. The autopsy will find no sign of rejection: the heart, for its part, was working.

The problem the operation had just solved, sewing a new heart into a chest, was not the one that killed Washkansky. The one that remained whole, keeping the immune system from treating a foreign organ as an intruder without destroying the patient's defenses along the way, would take years more to resolve. At the end of 1967, surgery had outpaced both the law and immunology at the same moment.

repere.texte: The report of the Harvard Medical School ad hoc committee charged with examining the definition of brain death, “A Definition of Irreversible Coma,” appeared in the Journal of the American Medical Association on August 5, 1968, eight months after the first human heart transplant.
repere.source: Ad Hoc Committee of the Harvard Medical School to Examine the Definition of Brain Death, “A Definition of Irreversible Coma,” JAMA, 205(6):337-340, August 5, 1968

carte.punch: In 1967, heart surgery was ready. The definition of brain death was not.
carte.idee: On December 3, 1967, in Cape Town, Christiaan Barnard transplants Denise Darvall's heart into Louis Washkansky. No law defined brain death: the team waits for the donor's heart to stop on its own. Washkansky dies eighteen days later, not of rejection but of pneumonia.

quiz.question: Why does Barnard's team wait for the donor's heart to stop on its own before removing it?
choix: Because the donor's family had not yet given consent to the removal
Because the surgical protocol required a safety delay after any road accident
Because no law yet defined brain death, and the team wanted to avoid any legal risk
Because a heart can never be removed before artificial respiration has completely stopped
quiz.explication: In 1967, no law anywhere in the world defined brain death: the Harvard criteria would not be published until August 1968. To avoid any legal risk, the team had a forensic pathologist certify the cardiac arrest before opening the chest.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What ultimately caused Louis Washkansky's death, eighteen days after the operation?
choix: Acute rejection of the graft, detected too late by the medical team
Pneumonia, worsened by the increase in immunosuppressants, wrongly ordered against a rejection that was not there
Internal bleeding caused by a late surgical complication
A lung infection transmitted directly by the transplanted heart
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The autopsy found no sign of rejection: the heart was working. The team had mistaken a lung infection for the onset of rejection and increased the immunosuppressants, which worsened the pneumonia.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who authorizes the removal of Denise Darvall's heart?
choix: A judge of the Cape Town court, urgently petitioned by the hospital
Denise Darvall herself, through a donor card found on her
Her father, after the neurosurgeon judged her brain injury hopeless
The South African Ministry of Health, through an exceptional authorization
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Her father gave consent to the removal of her heart after the neurosurgeon called in to treat her judged her brain injury hopeless. She herself was no longer in a state to decide.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the surgical technique Barnard uses to connect the graft come from?
choix: He invents it himself, in the weeks before the operation
It had already been developed in animals at Stanford University in the United States, by Norman Shumway and his team
It comes from a protocol published by the World Health Organization in 1965
It had already been tried on a first human patient in the Soviet Union in 1964
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Barnard and his brother had trained on dogs with a method described in London in 1959, then developed at Stanford University by Norman Shumway and his team, including Richard Lower. Barnard merely worked in Lower's laboratory, in Richmond.
